title: Mobile App Development Fundamentals
summary: Learn to plan, design and build mobile apps: native, cross-platform and PWA approaches, mobile-first design, screens and state with Flutter, APIs and offline sync, testing and performance, and publishing with privacy in mind.
audience: Programming learners, web developers moving to mobile and entrepreneurs planning an app

lessons.title: Platforms and ways to build apps

body.p: Most smartphones run Android or iOS. Android dominates in much of Africa and Asia, often on low-cost devices, while iOS has a large share in some richer markets. Know your users' devices before choosing how to build.

list: Native apps: Kotlin for Android, Swift for iOS. Best performance and full access to device features, but two code bases.
Cross-platform frameworks: Flutter (Dart) and React Native (JavaScript) build Android and iOS apps from one code base, with near-native performance for most apps.
Progressive web apps (PWAs): websites that can be installed, work offline and send notifications, with no app store needed; device access is more limited, especially on iOS.
Low-code tools: quick for simple internal apps, limited for complex ones.

body.p: A small team building a booking or learning app often starts with a cross-platform framework or a PWA. Games and apps that push the hardware may need native code or a game engine.

body.tip: Install Android Studio (and Xcode on a Mac for iOS) to get emulators, but always test on real, cheaper phones as well.

body.p: Mobile users are often busy, on the move, on small screens and on slow or expensive data. Design for one hand, short sessions and interruptions.

list: Touch targets of at least about 48 x 48 density-independent pixels on Android (44 points on iOS).
Put primary actions within thumb reach, usually near the bottom.
Follow platform conventions (Material Design on Android, Human Interface Guidelines on iOS) so the app feels familiar.
Keep text readable, support the system font-size setting and use strong contrast for bright sunlight.
Design for offline and slow networks: show cached content, queue actions and say clearly when something is waiting to sync.

body.p: App size matters. A 25 MB download costs a user on R80 per gigabyte about 25 / 1024 x 80, roughly R1.95, every time they install or update, and many phones are short of storage. Compress images, avoid unnecessary libraries and download large content only when needed.

body.tip: Test the main tasks with the phone in flight mode. Whatever breaks there will break for real users on weak signal.

body.p: Apps are built from screens made of widgets or components: text, images, buttons, lists and input fields. Navigation moves between screens, using stacks (push a detail screen, press back to return), tabs for main sections and drawers for less-used areas.

Everything in Flutter is a widget. CounterPage is stateful: it holds count, and calling setState tells Flutter to rebuild the screen so "Taps" shows the new value. React Native follows the same idea with components and the useState hook.

list: Keep screen widgets small and reusable.
Separate the user interface from business logic and data access so each can be tested.
For larger apps, use a state-management approach (such as Provider or Riverpod in Flutter, or a store in React Native) for data shared between screens.
Show loading, empty and error states on every screen that fetches data.

body.tip: Use hot reload during development: it shows code changes in seconds without losing the app's state.

lessons.title: Data, storage, APIs and offline sync

body.p: Most apps talk to a server through an API, usually over HTTPS with JSON. The app sends requests ("get my courses", "submit this order") and displays the responses. Treat the network as unreliable: set timeouts, retry sensibly and never assume a request succeeded until the server confirms.

list: Key-value storage for small settings, such as the chosen language.
A local database (such as SQLite) for structured data used offline.
Secure storage (Android Keystore, iOS Keychain) for tokens; never store passwords in plain text.
Files for downloaded media, cleaned up when no longer needed.

body.p: An offline-first app reads from local storage first and syncs with the server when a connection is available. Changes made offline are queued and sent later; the design must decide what happens if the same record was changed on two devices (a conflict).

body.tip: Never put secret API keys inside the app; apps can be unpacked. Keep secrets on your server and give each user their own short-lived token.

body.p: Users uninstall apps that crash, drain the battery or feel slow. Quality must be designed in, not added at the end.

list: Unit tests check logic such as price calculations.
Widget or component tests check individual screens.
Integration tests run real user flows on emulators and devices.
Test on a range of screen sizes, Android versions and a low-memory phone.
Run a beta through internal testing tracks before a full release.
Load large lists lazily and resize images to the size shown.
Avoid frequent background work and constant location tracking; batch network calls.
Measure startup time and frame rate with the platform's profiling tools.
Track crashes and errors with a crash-reporting tool. If 30 of 1000 sessions crash, the crash rate is 3%, far too high; aim well below 1%.

body.tip: Watch store reviews and crash reports daily after each release; most serious problems appear in the first hours.

body.p: Android apps are published on Google Play (a one-time developer registration fee) and iOS apps on Apple's App Store (an annual developer programme fee). Both review apps against their policies; Apple's review is usually stricter. Prepare an app icon, screenshots, a clear description and a privacy policy.

list: Paid apps: few users pay upfront in price-sensitive markets.

In-app purchases and subscriptions: the stores take a commission, commonly 15% for smaller developers and subscriptions after the first year, and 30% in other cases. On a R100 purchase, a 15% commission leaves R85 and 30% leaves R70.
Advertising: works at large scale but can annoy users and use their data.
Free app supporting a paid service, such as a booking or learning platform.

body.p: Ask for permissions (camera, location, contacts) only when needed, and explain why at that moment. Stores require you to declare what data you collect, and laws such as POPIA, the Nigeria Data Protection Act and GDPR apply. Measure retention: if 4200 of 10 000 installers are still active after a week, 42% retention, study where the others gave up.

body.tip: Release small updates often, with clear release notes, rather than rare giant updates.

quiz.q: Which approach builds Android and iOS apps from one code base?
options: A cross-platform framework such as Flutter

quiz.q: What is a progressive web app?
options: An installable website that can work offline

quiz.q: A minimum touch target on Android is about:
A 25 MB app at R80 per GB costs a user about how much to download?
Why test with the phone in flight mode?
options: To see how the app behaves offline or on weak signal

quiz.q: In the Flutter example, what does setState do?
options: Rebuilds the widget so the new count is shown

quiz.q: Why separate UI from business logic?
options: It removes the need for state
Each part can be tested and changed independently

quiz.q: Where should login tokens be stored on the device?
options: In secure storage such as Keystore or Keychain
Read from local storage first and sync when online

quiz.q: Why never embed secret API keys in an app?
options: Apps can be unpacked and the keys extracted

quiz.q: 30 of 1000 sessions crash. The crash rate is:
On a R100 in-app purchase with a 15% store commission, the developer receives:
When should an app ask for camera permission?
options: When the user first needs the camera, with an explanation
